title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Rep. Scholten pushes federal reporting rules as local opposition grows over power, water and taxes.

lines.text: Good evening, and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Tonight we're digging into a new federal push from Grand Rapids Democrat Hillary Scholten that could set national standards for how data centers report their water and energy use.
That's the big one today, Graham. Let's start there.

Scholten introduced two bills this morning that would require annual surveys of data center operators on their resource consumption and would update Defense Department cooling standards to better protect water supplies.
Why does this matter for Michigan right now, especially with all the local fights we're seeing?

Because Michigan has become a hotspot for these projects, and residents from Washtenaw to Kent County to the Thumb are already raising alarms about power demand, water drawdowns, and who pays for infrastructure upgrades.
The bills sound like they aim at transparency first. How would the reporting actually work?

Operators would have to disclose usage numbers every year, which could feed into state and local permitting decisions. The efficiency standards update targets cooling systems that currently can consume millions of gallons of water per facility.
And this comes the same day we learned 55 percent of Michigan primary voters oppose data centers near their homes, with even higher numbers among Democrats.
Exactly. That poll from yesterday shows the political pressure is real, and Scholten is responding by moving the conversation to Washington instead of leaving everything to township boards.
What about the history here? How long have these local battles been building?

They've been simmering for months across multiple counties, with pauses in places like Otsego and delays in Genesee. The common thread is residents worried about higher electric bills if big loads hit the grid without enough new generation.
DTE's filing today ties future rate stability directly to landing those large data center customers. So if the projects stall, do rates go up faster?
That's the utility's argument. They say the big loads help spread costs. Opponents counter that the campuses could drive up peak demand and force expensive upgrades that hit residential bills anyway.
Water is another flashpoint. How much are we talking about for a typical hyperscale site?

It varies, but cooling can pull hundreds of thousands of gallons daily in some designs. Scholten's bill tries to get better data so communities know what they're signing up for before approving projects.
And farmland and taxes come into it too. Some townships are offering big abatements while others worry about losing prime ag land or seeing property taxes shift.

Right. The recall effort filed today in Washtenaw against seven officials shows how personal these fights have become. Voters thirty miles away are watching to see if recalls actually reach the ballot and change who sits on those boards.
What happens next with Scholten's legislation? Does it have much chance in Congress?
It's early, but it gives Michigan a seat at the table on federal standards. Even if it doesn't pass quickly, it could shape how the industry and regulators talk about efficiency going forward.
Meanwhile, Senate candidate John James said Saturday he'd leave siting and tax decisions to locals rather than impose state rules.
That's a clear contrast. James wants townships like Saline and Coldwater to decide for themselves, which resonates in places already deep into negotiations.
And yesterday's poll shows opposition crossing party lines, so both sides are feeling the heat heading into tomorrow's primary.
Exactly. Now let's run through the rest of today's developments quickly.
In Dowagiac, Hyperscale Data is switching a site from Bitcoin mining to a 20-megawatt AI hosting contract worth over a billion dollars across ten years.
Residents there are still litigating noise complaints from the existing operation, so the change brings new questions about whether the power use stays the same or grows.
Genesee County postponed its environmental clearance vote for a proposed center, giving residents more time to review traffic, power, and noise impacts.
That extra review period could shape how the project moves forward or whether it gets scaled back.
Otsego city council voted Saturday to ban new data centers for a full year, giving the community breathing room to write its own rules.
Mason County is pitching itself as the home for Michigan's official state data center, competing with bigger metro areas for the construction jobs and tax base.
And in Coldwater, residents got their first public look at proposed projects at a joint meeting Friday, focusing on power, water, and tax break details.
Now for the one meeting listeners can actually attend tonight.
Delta County Planning Commission has its Data Center Subcommittee update and zoning ordinance discussion on the agenda this evening.
If you're in the area, that's a chance to hear the latest on local rules before anything advances.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker.
We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Scholten's Federal Bills Target Data Center Water and Power Use
